content_voiceover: This flowchart shows how the International Consensus Classification assigns diagnosis hierarchically once you have at least 10% myeloid blasts or blast equivalents. You work left to right through decreasing priority: first check for AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormalities, if absent, check for TP53 mutation with VAF at least 10%, if absent, check for the nine myelodysplasia-related gene mutations, if absent, check for myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities, and if all are negative, the diagnosis is AML not otherwise specified. At each of these last four branch points, the blast percentage then determines the final label: 10 to 19% blasts gives an MDS/AML diagnosis, while 20% or more gives the corresponding AML diagnosis. Only the first branch, AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormalities, bypasses this split and is called AML directly regardless of blast count. Finally, three diagnostic qualifiers can be appended to any of these diagnoses: therapy-related, arising after prior MDS or MDS/MPN, or associated with a germline predisposition syndrome. This hierarchy is exam-favorite material because it tests whether you understand that TP53 mutation status is checked before myelodysplasia-related mutations, meaning TP53 always takes priority.
keypoints: Order: AML-defining lesion -> TP53mut -> MDS-related mutation -> MDS-related cytogenetics -> NOS
Qualifiers: therapy-related, prior MDS, germline predisposition
keypoint_voiceover: Memorize the priority order: genetic-defining lesion first, then TP53, then myelodysplasia-related mutations, then cytogenetics, then NOS. Remember TP53 outranks the myelodysplasia-related gene panel.
